claims.text: At elevated temperature, the distinct phases in the eutectic HEA oxidize at different rates.
Differing phase-specific oxidation rates produce non-uniform, less-protective oxide scales.
Oxide heterogeneity is concentrated at phase boundaries because the constituent phases have different oxidation kinetics.
The heterogeneous oxide regions at phase boundaries are fragile and are removed preferentially by mechanical wear.
Wear-induced oxide removal repeatedly exposes fresh, dissimilar alloy phases.
Exposure of dissimilar phases creates localized galvanic cells along phase interfaces.
The localized galvanic cells accelerate corrosion.
Coupling wear-induced oxide removal with differential corrosion accelerates overall degradation.
A temperature around 500°C is sufficient for differential oxidation to become pronounced in the alloy.
A humid environment containing aggressive species such as chloride actively challenges oxide-layer integrity.
Lower-temperature conditions produce a more robust and homogeneous protective oxide scale than the elevated-temperature coupled condition.
Combined wear and corrosion at elevated temperature will cause super-additive total degradation relative to isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
The coupled elevated-temperature condition will increase localized-corrosion pit density relative to the proposed baseline.
The coupled elevated-temperature condition will increase wear-track depth relative to the proposed baseline.
Controlled thermal oxidation can produce a thermally stabilized, uniform oxide layer that inhibits differential oxidation effects.

If pre-oxidized samples retain a uniform oxide yet show degradation acceleration similar to untreated samples in both wear and corrosion, the proposed differential-oxidation mechanism is not supported.
